name: Upper Kuskokwim
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
sweep_summary: Upper Kuskokwim (uppe1438) is not in the catalog. The sweep's single bibliography item, Leer 1976 'Spirantization and the development of suprasegmentals in Proto-Athabaskan' (ANLA CA965L1976b), was fetched sources from ANLA (no text layer; scanned at 300 dpi, 86 pp.) and read: it is a comparative tonogenesis paper in which Upper Kuskokwim is only listed (ms. p. 11) among high-marked tone languages; it says nothing about word stress (and its tonal coding of UK was later contradicted by Scollon, Krauss and Kibrik, who find no or only vestigial low-marked tone). That surfaced one first-hand stress statement not on file: Scollon 1978, 'Note on pitch mostly in Upper Kuskokwim' (ANLA UK979S1979), fetched sources and read — no tone; 'Stress is stronger than vowel pitch. Penultimate stress in trisyllabic sequences will raise even a CV' syllable', with a pitch chart showing the penult raised in di- and trisyllables, and prefix pitch 'best treated as stress' (following Ray Collins). Kari 1978 (orthography tables) was also fetched sources: irrelevant. Kibrik's Word field files (PHON, TONE01, TONETEST etc.) were decoded and contain tone notes only. Everything fetched sources is and. Nothing relevant remains unread; no acquisition priorities.

new_statements.quote: 1) Upper Kuskokwim has no tone (at least in these forms) 2) Glottal stop depresses the pitch a) when it follows a vowel (CV' = V) b) not when it is glottalization on a consonant (CVC' = Ø) c) only when stress does not override it d) the sonorant n seems to act like V [...] 3) Stress is stronger than vowel pitch. Penultimate stress in trisyllabic sequences will raise even a CV' syllable. [chart: CV ⊣; CVCV ┐┤; CVCVCV(C) ┤┐┤; CV' ┘; (CV)CVCV' (┤)┐┘; CVCV'CV(C) ┤┐┤; CV'CV(C) ┘┤] ... I would be happy to go along with Ray Collins on Upper Kuskokwim in believing that pitch in prefixes is best treated as stress.
new_statements.citation: Scollon, Ronald. 1978. Note on pitch mostly in Upper Kuskokwim. Typescript memo, Alaska Native Language Center, October 16, 1978, 3 pp. ANLA UK979S1979 (catalogued as 1979). https://uafanlc.alaska.edu/Online/UK979S1979/
new_statements.locator: typescript p. 1 (PDF p. 4 of 5), points 1)-3) with pitch chart, and the closing paragraph
new_statements.reading: Word-level prominence is a pitch-realised stress on the penultimate syllable: in the chart the penult carries the high pitch in disyllables (CVCV: high-mid) and trisyllables (CVCVCV: mid-high-mid), and penultimate stress overrides the pitch lowering that a syllable-final glottal stop otherwise causes; the language has no lexical tone and prefix pitch is stress, not tone. Evidence base is thin: one consultant (Betty Petruska), Krauss's tone wordlist, a 3-page ANLC memo never published — so 'penultimate' is a first-hand but preliminary coding. No other opened source (Collins 1966/1979 dictionaries, Kibrik 1997-2025 papers and field files, Krauss 1979/1981, Leer 1976, Kari 1978) states where stress falls.

sources.citation: Kibrik, Andrej A. 1997/1998. Preliminary report on phonetic and phonological idiolectal variation in Upper Kuskokwim Athabaskan. Unpublished typescript, ANLA UK997K1998b; same text as PHON/PHON.DOC in the UK997K2001d field-notes zip (plus TONE01.DOC 'Tone explorations 2001', TONETEST.DOC).
sources.quote: Speakers like BP and WP do not seem to have any tone, and are comfortable with the monotonous pronunciation of words with expected tone countours. JG seems to have weak tone differences. [...] He operates pretty much on the basis of the low marked hypothesis, but has downdrift in the closed final syllables.
sources.note: Tone (vestigial, low-marked, idiolectal) only; none of Kibrik's phonology files (PHON, TONE01, TONETEST, DIALECT, CONS-01, WALS-QU, FAIRBX01, JAGOLA) mentions stress or accent.

sources.citation: Krauss, Michael E. 1981. [Notes on Upper Kuskokwim tone.] Ms. dated March 19, 1981, 1 p. (elicitation with Miska Deaphon and Agnes Tony, Fairbanks). ANLA UK961K1981.
sources.quote: very toneless! ... no verb stem tone — no noun stem tone ... definitely non-tonal, but vestige of tone, if any, indicates low-markedness [my reading of Krauss's hand]
sources.note: Handwritten elicitation notes: 'very toneless!'; no stress remarks.

sources.citation: Krauss, Michael E. 1979 [2005]. Athabaskan tone. In Sharon Hargus & Keren Rice (eds.), Athabaskan Prosody, 55-136. Amsterdam: Benjamins (2003 typeset preprint, ANLA CA961K1978).
sources.quote: Of the rest of the Athabaskan languages, Babine-Hagwilgate in Canada (on evidence from James Kari) and in Alaska, Ahtna, Tanaina, Ingalik, Upper Kuskowin [sic] and the Central and Upper dialects Koyukon are definitely toneless [...] The remaining Alaskan languages, Upper Tanana, Tanacross, Tanana, Upper Kuskokwim, and at least the Lower dialect (and probably Upper dialect) of Koyukon, have tone systems of a sort, as yet poorly understood.
sources.locator: sec. 7.2 'Carrier and Alaskan tone' (preprint p. 61) and sec. 2 (p. 9)
sources.note: Tone only; Upper Kuskokwim appears (inconsistently) in both the 'definitely toneless' and the 'tone systems of a sort' lists. No statement of stress placement for this language.

sources.citation: Scollon, Ronald. 1978 [ANLA catalogues it as 1979]. Note on pitch mostly in Upper Kuskokwim. Typescript memo, Alaska Native Language Center, dated October 16, 1978, 3 pp. (+ Krauss cover note 1/29/79 and a handwritten elicitation sheet 'Jan 25 1979'). ANLA UK979S1979. [found via the ANLA API listing of the 130 online UK items; not in the sweep list]
sources.quote: 1) Upper Kuskokwim has no tone (at least in these forms) 2) Glottal stop depresses the pitch a) when it follows a vowel (CV' = V) b) not when it is glottalization on a consonant (CVC' = Ø) c) only when stress does not override it [...] 3) Stress is stronger than vowel pitch. Penultimate stress in trisyllabic sequences will raise even a CV' syllable. [chart: CV ⊣; CVCV ┐┤; CVCVCV(C) ┤┐┤; CV' ┘; (CV)CVCV' (┤)┐┘; CVCV'CV(C) ┤┐┤; CV'CV(C) ┘┤] [...] For the moment I would be happy to go along with Ray Collins on Upper Kuskokwim in believing that pitch in prefixes is best treated as stress.
sources.locator: typescript p. 1 = PDF p. 4 of 5, points 1)-3) and the pitch chart; final paragraph same page
sources.note: First-hand elicitation (Krauss's Athabaskan-tone wordlist, consultant Betty Petruska of Nikolai, recorded with Ray Collins): no tone; a pitch-realised stress that falls on the PENULTIMATE syllable — the chart shows the penult raised in disyllables and trisyllables, and the raising overrides the pitch depression of a glottal stop; pitch differences on prefixes are stress, not tone (agreeing with Collins). One speaker, a 3-page ANLC memo, not a published analysis.

sources.citation: Leer, Jeff. 1976. Spirantization and the Development of Suprasegmentals in Proto-Athabaskan. Ms. dated 7-21-76 (24 pp.) + typescript (30 pp.). ANLA CA965L1976b. [Glottolog ref 167470; the sweep's only bibliography item]
sources.quote: In Kutchin, Tanana, Upper Kuskokwim, Sarcee and Navajo as well as other languages not included in this study, the reflex of V̓ is high tone and the reflex of v is low tone. In Chipewyan and other Canadian languages the reflex of V̓ is low tone and the reflex of v is high tone. [scanned renders Leer's constricted/plain vowel symbols as 'Vv' and 'v']
sources.locator: ms. p. 11 (PDF p. 15; repeated in the typescript at PDF p. 45); Upper Kuskokwim is otherwise only named in a list of retroflex-series languages, ms. p. 5 (PDF p. 9)
sources.note: Nothing about word stress. The paper is a comparative tonogenesis proposal (Proto-Athabaskan vowel nuclei > modern tone, prompted by Tongass Tlingit and Eyak); Upper Kuskokwim appears only as one name in a list of 'high-marked' tone languages. Note that this 1976 classification of UK as tonal was later contradicted by Scollon 1978, Krauss 1979/2005 and Krauss 1981 (no tone) and by Kibrik 1997-2001 (vestigial LOW-marked tone in some idiolects).
